# Discrete and continuous number {#sec-discreteContinuous}

<!-- {{< include ../preamble.qmd >}} -->

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
To count or to measure.
:::

The title of this chapter should be natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ and real numbers $\mathbb{R}$. Everyone is familiar with these sets. Because the set of natural numbers is a subset of real numbers, one can basically use real number and ignore the set of natural numbers.

So why such a title and why the distinction? The answer to the first question is because this book is about applied mathematics and more an emphasis about the properties than nomenclature. In other words, natural numbers has the properties of discrete, while real numbers is a continuous set. The difference between discrete and continuous will appear in the statistics parts (discrete and continuous variables @sec-quantitative-variable) and again implemented differently in [programming language](@sec-numeric).

## Formal {.unnumbered}
The formal definition is useless in the purpose of this book (unless you want to learn about topology).
It could describe in the following, a discrete discrete set, every number is isolated.
In contrast, in a continuous, any number has a neighbor. And this is true no matter how close one looks.
That is why a continuous number (real number) is represented by a continuous line where as natural number should be points.


## Examples {.unnumbered}
- World of discrete numbers: Odd (2, 4, 6, 8 etc) and even (3, 5, 7, 9 etc.), prime numbers (3, 5, 7, 11, etc), and also the negative mirror.

- World of continuous numbers: $\pi = 3.14\ldots$, $e = 2.71\ldots$, $\sqrt{2}$ and the fractions

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Semantic: whole number, natural number, integer while the later includes mirror negative
- Discrete number is mostly used for counting and indexing (e.g. in summation and product @sec-sum)
- Tools to are fundamentaly different.
  -  For instance, using[difference equation](@sec-difference) to model when time is discrete and [differential equation](@sec-differential) when time is continuous.
  -  In probabilites, a sum is used to compute the mean if the variable is discrete, an integral is used if the variable is continuous
